extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of classical geometry / mathematicians studying Archimedean constructions
extracted.subtask_description: Geometric constructions and existence conditions for cutting a sphere by a plane to produce segments with prescribed relationships (volumes, surfaces, similarity), and related results on circle measurement. Includes analytic elimination, reduction to cones, and use of conics to locate division points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cone equals segment (Prop. 2 construction criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: If H is taken on OA produced so that OA' + A'M : A'M = HM : MA (and similarly for H' on OA' produced), then the cone with vertex H and base the circle on BB' as diameter is equal to the spherical segment ABB'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used repeatedly: choose points H, H' on OA, OA' produced satisfying OA'+A'M:A'M = HM:MA and OA+AM:AM = H'M:MA'. Then the cones HBB', H'BB' are respectively equal to the segments ABB', A'BB' [Prop. 2]. This provides a reduction of segment-volume problems to cone-height/ratio problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct plane giving segments in given volume ratio (Prop. 4 synthesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: To cut a sphere by a plane so that the volumes of the segments are to one another in a given ratio R:S, produce OA to D so OA = AD, divide AD in E so AE : ED = R : S, then cut AA' in M so that MD : DE = AA" : A'M'. Through M erect a plane perpendicular to AA' — this plane will divide the sphere into segments in the ratio R:S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes' synthesis: produce OA to D with OA = AD; choose E on AD with AE:ED = R:S; find M on AA' with MD:DE = AA":A'M' (constructed from cones equal to segments via Prop. 2). The analysis/elimination (finding H, H' and equating compounded ratios) justifies these steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subsidiary division problem (AM:AC = D : MB') — existence condition and method
rubrics_metrics.description: Given two straight lines AB, AC and an area D, divide AB at M so that AM : AC = D : MB'. Analysis reduces to finding the intersection P of a given parabola and a given rectangular hyperbola; M is obtained from P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maximum of AM·MB' occurs when BM = 2·AM; hence a necessary condition for a solution is that AC·D must not exceed the maximum (expressed in the text as AC·D ≤ AO·OB' in the configuration with O such that BO = 2·AO). If AC·D equals the maximum O is the solution; if AC·D is less there are two intersections (two solutions). Construction: place AC at right angles to AB, construct the parallelogram/rectangles as in the analysis, then draw the parabola (vertex F, axis EV, parameter = EL) and the rectangular hyperbola (asymptotes CH, CF) which intersect at P; drop PM parallel to AC to find M.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of conics to locate division points (general method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine points (such as M or P) as intersections of appropriately constructed conics: parabola and rectangular hyperbola (or ellipse and hyperbola in other reductions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes (via Eutocius et al.) reduces cubic/division problems to geometric intersections: e.g., construct a parabola with given vertex/axis/parameter and a rectangular hyperbola with given asymptotes/passing through a point; their intersection P determines M. Similarly, ellipse-hyperbola intersections occur in Diocles' approach. The text gives explicit constructions of these conics from given segments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence / multiplicity conclusions from inequality comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a geometrical division problem has zero, one, or two positive solutions depends on inequalities between given quantities (products/ratios).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for the subsidiary problem AC·D compared to the critical value AO·OB' (with BO = 2·AO): if equal, one solution (O); if less, two solutions (two intersections of conics); if greater, no solution (impossibility shown via extremal product arguments). Archimedes explicitly proves and invokes such necessary conditions (διορισμός).

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary condition for segment-to-cone ratio construction (Prop. 7)
rubrics_metrics.description: To cut off a spherical segment whose volume has a given ratio to the cone with the same base and equal height, the given ratio must be greater than 3 : 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: OA' + A'A : A'A = 3 : 2 (for the hemisphere case), so any attainable HM:MA (ratio of cone heights that equals the required ratio) must exceed 3 : 2. The synthesis takes a line with the given ratio (>3:2) and finds M accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of segment surfaces equivalent to equality of diameters (I.42,43 reference)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two spherical segments have equal surface areas then the circles on their diameters (i.e., the diameters of their bases) are equal; in particular, equal segment surfaces imply equal base diameters (AB = DE in the text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in constructions seeking a segment similar to one given and having surface equal to another (Prop. 6): since surfaces equal ⇒ base diameters equal, one can fix the required base diameter for the new segment and then choose the cut so that similarity holds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing a segment similar to one and equal in volume to another (Prop. 5 method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given two segments ABB' and DEF, to construct def similar to DEF and equal in volume to ABB': reduce segments to equal cones via Prop. 2, relate diameters and heights (mean proportionals), choose ef and S such that ef and S are two mean proportionals in continued proportion between BB' and R (constructed from KG:EF = HM:R), then build segment on ef similar to DEF.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: from cone-equality relationships obtain ratios leading to two mean proportionals; then on the chosen mean-proportional ef construct the circular segment similar to DEF and erect the corresponding sphere section to obtain def. The text gives algebraic ratio steps to determine ef and S.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing a segment similar to one and equal in surface to another (Prop. 6 synthesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given segment ABB' whose surface will equal that of required segment similar to DEF: choose d'd such that d'd : AB = D'D : DF, then on d'd as diameter construct the circle and plane perpendicular to its diameter at appropriate point to cut off def similar to DEF and with df = AB, hence surface equality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses the equivalence of circle-diameter equality with equality of segment surfaces and the similarity ratios between corresponding parts; explicit steps to choose d'd and divide it at g so that similarity and surface equality hold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequalities relating volumes and surface areas of complementary segments (Prop. 8 statement)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a sphere is cut by a plane producing two segments A'BB' (greater) and ABB' (lesser), then the ratio (segmt. A'BB') : (segmt. ABB') is less than (surface of A'BB')^? : (surface of ABB')^? but greater than (surface of A'BB')^* : (surface of ABB')^*.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes expresses the comparison in terms of powers/compounded ratios of the surface measures; the passage (text as printed) reads: 'then the ratio (segmt. A’BB’): (segmt. ABB’) < (surface of A’BB’)’ : (surface of ABB'Y but > (surface of A’BB’)*: (surface of ABB’)™*.' The argument proceeds by reducing segments to cones and using the relationships HM, H'M to A'M, AM (via Prop. 2 relations) to bound the volume ratio between functions of the surface ratio.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hemisphere maximizes volume among segments with equal surface (Prop. 9)
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all spherical segments having equal surfaces, the hemisphere encloses the greatest volume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: equate surface (so base diameters equal), produce points H with OA' = A'K and use cone = segment relations to compare cone volumes; deduce hemisphere (cone corresponding to a full diameter) has larger cone (hence segment) volume than any other segment with the same surface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Area of a circle equals a right triangle with sides radius and circumference (Measurement Proposition 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The area of any circle is equal to the area of a right-angled triangle in which one of the sides about the right angle is equal to the radius and the other to the circumference of the circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes proves this by inscribing and circumscribing polygons and showing contradictions if the circle-area were greater or less than the stated triangle; uses polygonal approximations and comparisons of perimeters and perpendiculars from center to polygon sides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounds on the ratio circumference : diameter (Measurement Proposition 9)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ratio of the circumference of any circle to its diameter is less than 22/7 but greater than 3 + 10/71 (Archimedes' classical bounds on π).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes obtains these bounds by constructing regular polygons (e.g., 96-gon) inscribed/circumscribed and using successive angle bisections with explicit rational approximations; the text records a sequence of bisectors and inequalities leading to the numerical bounds.
